title: “Bat Out Of Hell” would like a word #broadway #musicaltheatre #lostboys
transcript: here's my take on the divisive Lost Boys musical I'll go into detail as I always do but I can kind of sum it up by saying: the highs were really high but there weren't enough of them. there were scattered moments throughout the production where they're either leaning into the horror spectacle with the impressive and very expensive stagecraft and/or, the high melodrama fueled by the bombastic rock score. and in those moments I felt like I was watching some of the best content of the Broadway season but it also felt at odds with the rest of the production and like, the whole show is corny, right? but it's corny in two different ways at different times like yeah you have rockstar vampires flying through the air and riding motorcycles but that's the kind of silly that I was totally on board for because it's indulging in this larger than life operaticism, almost it's when we get into the sort of Disney Channel humor and the sort of off-brand Dear Evan Hansen family dramedy that I was less on board and in both cases I'm not expecting great writing from the book or the lyrics but I'm more willing to forgive that when it's more campy than goofy and not only do I think the percentage was skewed in the wrong direction the sense of whiplash was, in itself, frustrating to experience I was also kinda disappointed to learn that four of the songs (and really 3 of the best songs) were repurposed from the existing catalogue of the Rescues the band that wrote it. and to be very clear the reason I'm disappointed isn't because I have a problem with them doing that it's not even because I thought they did it badly it's only disappointing because I wanted to give this musical more credit for the parts of the score that I really vibed with and this just means that there is a lower percentage of original songs that I feel inclined to praise cause much like the book and the direction the score also feels split between the high octane pop/rock opera feel versus a more conventional, contemporary musical theatre sound and I guess it makes sense for the vampires and the non-vampires to have a different sound I just found one style a lot more to my taste than the other last two aspects of the show that I wanna talk about are both more specific, and more positive but I think they speak to the larger point I've been making: first of all, I loved Ali Louis Bourzgui as the main vampire guy it was such a captivating performance that was allowed to be weird and idiosyncratic in a way that I wish more musical theater performances were allowed to be these days. second and finally there was this little flourish at the very end of the production that, to me, was a great example of leaning into this popcorn entertainment feel but in ways that imaginatively play around with a traditional Broadway format and again I just wish the show had more of that
reasoning: Weinberg articulates a clearly mixed take: high highs but too few of them, tonal whiplash, and disappointment with much of the score, balanced against praise for the lead performance and specific moments. He neither recommends nor discourages.
